title: Uterine fibroids
intro: Fibroids are non-cancerous growths in the muscle wall of the womb. They are very common, and many women never know they have them. When they cause heavy periods, pain or pressure, there are many treatment options, from medicines to surgery.

sections.heading: What fibroids are
paragraphs: Fibroids vary in size from tiny to as large as a melon, and may be single or multiple. They are described by location: within the wall, under the lining, bulging into the cavity or on the outside surface. Their growth depends on oestrogen and progesterone, so they often grow during reproductive years and shrink after menopause. Family history, being overweight and African ancestry raise risk.

sections.heading: Symptoms
paragraphs: Many women have none. Common symptoms are heavy or prolonged periods that may cause anaemia, period pain, pelvic pressure or fullness, frequent urination, constipation, back pain, pain during sex and, sometimes, difficulty conceiving or pregnancy complications. Sudden severe pain can happen if a fibroid loses blood supply or is twisted.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
paragraphs: Fibroids are found during pelvic examination, and confirmed by ultrasound. MRI may help plan treatment. Blood tests check for anaemia. Fibroids that are not causing problems usually need no treatment, only occasional review. Cancer in a fibroid is extremely rare.

sections.heading: Treatment options
paragraphs: For heavy bleeding, options include hormonal coils, tablets that reduce bleeding, hormonal treatments that shrink fibroids for a time, and iron for anaemia. Procedures include removing fibroids while keeping the womb (myomectomy), blocking their blood supply with embolisation, ablation with heat or ultrasound energy and hysterectomy, which removes the womb and permanently resolves the problem. Choice depends on symptoms, size, location, age and wishes about pregnancy.

sections.heading: Fertility and pregnancy
paragraphs: Most women with fibroids conceive and have normal pregnancies. Fibroids that distort the cavity may reduce fertility or raise the risk of miscarriage, and large ones can cause complications at delivery. Discuss plans for pregnancy before treatment, since some procedures may influence it.

examples.title: Describing your periods
examples.text: Imagine your periods have become heavy and long. You could keep a record of days and pad changes, and bring it to your appointment.

examples.title: Comparing options
examples.text: Suppose you want to keep your womb. You might ask your gynaecologist about myomectomy and embolisation, and what each means for fertility.
